newsitem.title: UK: Gulf Canada bid for Clyde too low - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada bid for Clyde too low - analysts.

text.p: Industry analysts believe Gulf Canada Resources Ltd will have to better its offer for Clyde Petroleum Plc to secure its planned takeover of the British oil exploration and production firm.
"The share price is telling you -- and I tend to agree -- that this bid is not going to be enough," said Nick Antill at brokers BZW.
In early afternoon trading, Clyde shares were up 36-1/2 pence at 121 pence compared with Gulf Canada's bid of 105 pence a share.
Industry watchers believe a "white knight" topping Gulf Canada's bid may well appear as many larger oil firms are looking to replace reserves and have the money to do so via an acquisition.
"The whole industry is in a state of a flux and certainly you could not rule out another interested party," said Kleinwort Benson's Paul Spedding.
A flurry of takeovers started about a year ago when Norway's Statoil bought Ireland's Aran with Mobil Corp giving extra momentum shortly afterwards as it launched a bid for Australia's Ampolex Ltd.
Aquisitions then followed across the globe, but mainly centred on mature areas such as the North Sea and South East Asia.
"There clearly is a hunger for these kind of assets," said Spedding.
Many bigger oil firms have moved onto the takeover trail as they turned cash-flow positive after years of cost-cutting.
At the same time they have difficulties replacing their oil and gas reserves through discoveries, giving them an added impetus to start buying assets instead.
One of the last deals was Saga Petroleum ASA which earlier this month bought Santa Fe Exploration, active in the UK part of the North Sea, from Kuwait Petroleum Exploration.
Many more acquisitions will undoubtedly follow, but analysts are reluctant to name potential takeover targets.
They stress that some predators may be looking for mature blocks -- such as owned by Clyde --, while others could be keen on buying assets where most of the potential still needs to be unlocked.
"The beauty lies in the eye of the beholder," said analyst Irene Himona at SocGen.
One rough rule of thumb is to consider those shares cheap which trade at a premium smaller than say 20 percent to their net asset value, said Antill.
On that basis, Cairn Energy Plc and Hardy Oil & Gas Plc look inexpensive, he added.

But given the different tastes of potential buyers as well as difficulties in calculating the net asset value, Antill hastens to say that cheap does not mean a company also qualifies as a takeover target.
"It is very difficult just to read across and say: "well somebody is prepared to pay "x' for Clyde, then somebody else should pay "y' for another company'," he said.
